$440 because the domestic intermediate value is added again.

Foreign production enters U.S. GDP when the resulting goods or services are eventually sold to U.S. consumers

expectedAfter.feedback: GDP is domestic production. Income earned abroad relates more to national income measures, not U.S. GDP.

expectedAfter.q: Imported prescription-drug prices rise while prices of domestic hospital services are unchanged. Which outcome is plausible?
options: GDP-deflator inflation must exceed CPI inflation

expectedAfter.feedback: Imported prescription drugs can raise the CPI because they are consumer purchases. They are not domestic production, so they do not directly raise the GDP deflator; unchanged domestic hospital prices add no offsetting price increase.

records.questionSet: Inflation Measurement and Real Values — Practice

expectedAfter.q: Prices of domestically produced aircraft exports rise while imported smartphones bought by households become cheaper. Which combination is plausible?
options: The GDP deflator rises while the CPI falls
The CPI rises while the GDP deflator falls
Both indexes must rise because one price increased
Both indexes must fall because consumers buy smartphones
expectedAfter.feedback: The aircraft exports are domestic production and enter the GDP deflator, so their higher prices push it up. Imported smartphones enter the CPI but not the GDP deflator; their lower price can pull CPI inflation down.

expectedAfter.q: Individual prices are unchanged, but current domestic production shifts toward goods with higher relative prices. Why can the GDP deflator change?
options: Its fixed consumer basket must be replaced every month
It includes every imported consumer purchase automatically
Its value is determined only by household expenditure shares
Its weights reflect the composition of current domestic output
expectedAfter.feedback: The GDP deflator weights prices by the composition of current domestic output. When production shifts toward goods with higher relative prices, the weighted price index can change even if each individual price is unchanged.

expectedAfter.q: Consumer import prices fall, domestic export prices rise, and output shifts toward exports. Why might the GDP deflator rise as CPI falls?

CPI assigns all weight to domestic exports
The deflator measures consumer purchasing power only
Coverage and current-output weights reinforce the divergence
expectedAfter.feedback: Falling consumer-import prices can lower CPI, while rising prices for domestic exports raise the GDP deflator. A shift in output toward exports gives those higher domestic-export prices more weight in the deflator.

expectedAfter.feedback: Domestic transit vehicles are newly produced domestic output, so their prices enter the GDP deflator. Imported fuel bought by households is in the consumer basket and can enter CPI, but it is not domestic production.
